concepts.title: Many organizations, one weather picture
concepts.explain: Aviation weather service combines observations and forecasts from the National Weather Service, FAA, other government agencies, and weather-reporting networks. Each product answers a different question.
concepts.apply: Compare a current airport observation with a forecast for your estimated arrival. They are not interchangeable.

concepts.title: Observation versus forecast
concepts.explain: An observation describes conditions actually measured or seen at a particular time and place. A forecast predicts conditions for a later time or wider area and contains uncertainty.
concepts.apply: The arrival airport METAR is a snapshot now; its TAF is one source for later arrival conditions.

concepts.title: Why data ages
concepts.explain: Weather changes after a report is taken. Collection, processing, transmission, and display all add delays; a current-looking screen can show old observations.
concepts.apply: Always check observation time and product validity before relying on a displayed report.

concepts.title: Use multiple independent sources
concepts.explain: Surface reports, radar, satellite data, pilot reports, and forecasts cover different phenomena and time scales. One source rarely gives the full route picture.
concepts.apply: Before a cross-country, examine departure, route, destination, alternates, and the trend instead of checking a single airport.

concepts.title: A briefing supports a decision
concepts.explain: The pilot combines relevant reports with personal minimums, aircraft capability, terrain, fuel, and alternates. A product alone does not declare a flight safe.
concepts.apply: If the data are conflicting or incomplete, seek clarification, delay, or choose another plan.

check.question: Which product tells you what is occurring at an airport right now?
check.explanation: A METAR reports observed surface conditions. A TAF forecasts conditions for a future period.

title: Surface, Upper-Air, Radar and Satellite Observations

concepts.title: Surface observations
concepts.explain: Airport weather stations report wind, visibility, weather, clouds, temperature, dew point, and pressure. Automated systems may have limitations, especially for phenomena they cannot detect.
concepts.apply: Treat automated observation data as useful but not an exhaustive description of nearby weather.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-1 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Upper-air measurements
concepts.explain: Balloon and other upper-air data reveal temperature, humidity, pressure, and winds above the surface. These measurements help forecast development and the flight environment.
concepts.apply: A cloud deck may be connected to an upper-level temperature and moisture pattern invisible from the ramp.

concepts.title: Weather radar
concepts.explain: Radar detects returned energy from precipitation particles. Echo intensity can highlight heavier precipitation but does not directly measure all turbulence or icing.
concepts.apply: Avoid treating a green or empty radar patch as a guarantee of smooth, safe air.

concepts.title: Satellite imagery
concepts.explain: Satellites help show cloud patterns and the development and movement of large weather systems. Their images complement observations taken close to the ground.
concepts.apply: A satellite view may reveal an approaching cloud shield that a single local METAR cannot describe.

concepts.title: Radar and satellite are not winds aloft
concepts.explain: These products describe different variables. Winds aloft forecasts and pilot reports are more direct aids to anticipating flight-level winds and turbulence.
concepts.apply: Choose a source that measures or forecasts the phenomenon you need, instead of assuming one picture answers everything.

check.question: Which is the best interpretation of precipitation radar?
options: It directly proves there is no turbulence
It detects precipitation echoes, not all hazards
check.explanation: Precipitation intensity is not a universal indicator of icing, turbulence, or ceiling height.

concepts.title: Prepare the flight details
concepts.explain: A useful briefing needs the departure and destination, route, proposed time, expected altitude, aircraft type, and intended flight rules.
concepts.apply: Tell the briefer your actual route and planned altitude rather than simply asking whether it is good weather.

concepts.title: Standard briefing
concepts.explain: The chapter describes the standard briefing as a broad review for a proposed flight, including adverse conditions, synopsis, current conditions, forecasts, and advisories.
concepts.apply: For an approaching departure, a standard briefing helps build the complete risk picture.

concepts.title: Abbreviated briefing
concepts.explain: An abbreviated briefing updates specific items or supplements information you already have. It does not replace a full review when essential information was never checked.
concepts.apply: After a delay, request or obtain updates to the older information.

concepts.title: Outlook briefing
concepts.explain: An outlook briefing is used when the flight is several hours away and more specific reports will be available nearer departure.
concepts.apply: For tomorrow’s flight, use the outlook to plan, then obtain a newer briefing closer to launch.

concepts.title: Briefings continue in flight
concepts.explain: A preflight briefing is not the end of weather decision-making. Obtain updates and amend the plan when changes affect safety.
concepts.apply: When conditions move faster than expected, reassess en route rather than holding to the original plan.

check.question: You already received a briefing but your departure is delayed. What is most helpful?
check.explanation: An updated or abbreviated briefing helps identify changes since the previous information.

title: Decode a METAR: The Basic Structure

concepts.title: Station and report time
concepts.explain: A METAR starts with an airport identifier and observation timestamp in UTC. Example training string: METAR KDEN 151753Z. This means the report was issued for the 15th at 17:53 UTC.
concepts.apply: Compare the date and UTC time with your expected departure time before reading other values.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-5 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Wind group
concepts.explain: A wind group such as 22012G20KT represents wind FROM 220° true at 12 knots, gusting to 20 knots. VRB can show variable direction.
concepts.apply: Use runway orientation and gusts to assess crosswind components and control margins.

concepts.title: Visibility group
concepts.explain: In US METARs, 6SM denotes six statute miles of prevailing visibility. Low visibility can be a limiting condition despite a high cloud base.
concepts.apply: Distinguish visibility from ceiling when evaluating VFR suitability.

concepts.title: Cloud and ceiling groups
concepts.explain: FEW, SCT, BKN, and OVC describe increasing sky coverage. BKN020 means a broken layer with its base 2,000 feet above the airport; a broken or overcast layer can establish a ceiling.
concepts.apply: Do not interpret BKN020 as 2,000 feet MSL. It is reported as height above the observation site.

concepts.title: Temperature, dew point and altimeter
concepts.explain: 18/12 means temperature 18°C and dew point 12°C. A2992 gives altimeter setting 29.92 inches of mercury. Other remarks may contain important detail.
concepts.apply: Read the entire report, especially current altimeter setting and changes in temperature/dew-point spread.

check.question: What does BKN020 describe in a US METAR?
options: Broken clouds based at 2,000 feet above station
check.explanation: BKN is broken sky cover, and 020 means a 2,000-foot cloud base above the observation site.

title: METAR Weather Codes and Special Reports

concepts.title: Precipitation codes
concepts.explain: RA means rain, SN means snow, and DZ means drizzle. A leading minus sign indicates light and a plus sign indicates heavy intensity for applicable phenomena.
concepts.apply: In the example -RA, the observation reports light rain; it is not a forecast of rain.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-5 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Obscuration codes
concepts.explain: BR indicates mist and FG indicates fog. Other codes describe haze, dust, and smoke. Each has different operational implications.
concepts.apply: A changing report from BR to FG may signal a major visibility problem.

concepts.title: Convective descriptors
concepts.explain: TS indicates thunderstorms and SH indicates showers. These codes describe weather near the reporting station, not the entire route.
concepts.apply: Use radar and advisories too when a METAR reports a thunderstorm.

concepts.title: SPECI is a special observation
concepts.explain: A SPECI is issued when certain weather changes meet reporting criteria between routine METAR observations.
concepts.apply: If the destination conditions are changing rapidly, watch for special reports rather than waiting for the next routine observation.

concepts.title: Put the groups together
concepts.explain: Training example: METAR KABC 151755Z 22012KT 6SM -RA BKN020 18/12 A2992. This fictional report gives a time, wind, visibility, light rain, broken clouds, temperature/dew point, and pressure.
concepts.apply: Decode a full report as a whole; a single favorable number does not make all conditions acceptable.

check.question: In a METAR, what does -RA mean?
check.explanation: The minus sign marks light intensity. RA denotes rain.

concepts.title: Why PIREPs are valuable
concepts.explain: PIREPs are firsthand reports from aircraft in flight. They can describe actual icing, turbulence, cloud tops, visibility, and other conditions that forecast models may miss.
concepts.apply: A recent report near your altitude is a strong cue to reassess the expected ride.

concepts.title: Read location, time and altitude
concepts.explain: A useful PIREP identifies a position, observation time and altitude. Without matching these fields, a hazard report may be misapplied.
concepts.apply: Icing reported at 9,000 feet should not automatically be treated as identical at every other altitude.

concepts.title: Report turbulence correctly
concepts.explain: Turbulence descriptions use standardized intensity and may specify the duration and altitude. Severity can depend on aircraft response and occupant effects.
concepts.apply: Avoid approximating turbulence intensity from radar echo color.

concepts.title: Report icing conditions
concepts.explain: Icing reports describe icing type, intensity, and relevant flight conditions. Temperature alone cannot establish whether airframe ice is present.
concepts.apply: A report of moderate icing on your route may require rerouting or cancelling, depending on aircraft approval.

concepts.title: Share reports and compare sources
concepts.explain: PIREPs improve weather awareness for other pilots and forecasters. They are spot reports, not full-route guarantees.
concepts.apply: A lack of PIREPs is not proof the air is free of hazards.

check.question: A PIREP reports severe turbulence 10 miles ahead at your altitude. What is the sound response?
options: Ignore it because radar shows light precipitation
Treat it as relevant risk information and alter plans
check.explanation: Actual pilot reports are relevant observations. Consider altitude, location, time, and options before proceeding.

title: TAF: Forecast Weather at an Airport

concepts.title: A TAF is a forecast, not observation
concepts.explain: A Terminal Aerodrome Forecast describes expected conditions for a defined airport area and validity period. It uses many familiar METAR-style codes.
concepts.apply: Use the destination TAF for expected arrival weather but continue checking actual reports.

concepts.title: Issuance and validity
concepts.explain: Read the airport identifier, issuance timestamp, and validity interval. A forecast for the wrong time can mislead a go/no-go decision.
concepts.apply: Compare your planned arrival time in UTC to the TAF forecast period.

concepts.title: FM groups
concepts.explain: FM (from) marks a forecast change beginning at the specified UTC time. Conditions after that group replace the prior prevailing forecast.
concepts.apply: If your arrival straddles an FM transition, consider the possible shift before landing.

concepts.title: TEMPO groups
concepts.explain: TEMPO indicates expected temporary fluctuations during the specified window. They can still be operationally important.
concepts.apply: Temporary low visibility during your approach window deserves attention even if the prevailing forecast looks good.

concepts.title: Forecast uncertainty
concepts.explain: A TAF summarizes expected conditions over a period and can be amended. It is not a promise that conditions will change on the minute.
concepts.apply: Always compare it with METARs, trends, and the latest amendments.

check.question: What is the main difference between METAR and TAF?
check.explanation: METAR is an observation and TAF is a terminal forecast.

concepts.title: Advisories flag significant hazards
concepts.explain: AIRMETs and SIGMETs communicate weather phenomena that may affect aircraft operations across broader areas. They should be read with times, boundaries, and altitudes.
concepts.apply: A route crossing an advisory area warrants a detailed look at its specific hazard.

concepts.title: AIRMET Sierra
concepts.explain: In the handbook, AIRMET Sierra covers IFR conditions and mountain obscuration. Both may affect terrain clearance and visual navigation.
concepts.apply: Mountain obscuration can be dangerous even if the weather at the nearest low-elevation airport looks manageable.

concepts.title: AIRMET Tango
concepts.explain: AIRMET Tango covers turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 knots or greater, and low-level wind shear conditions.
concepts.apply: Factor turbulence and wind shear into route, altitude, and aircraft selection.

concepts.title: AIRMET Zulu
concepts.explain: AIRMET Zulu addresses icing and freezing level information. Aviation icing depends on temperature and visible moisture, among other conditions.
concepts.apply: For an aircraft without icing approval, an icing advisory is a serious reason to avoid affected conditions.

concepts.title: SIGMET and convective SIGMET
concepts.explain: SIGMETs warn of weather potentially hazardous to all aircraft, including severe or extreme turbulence and severe icing. Convective SIGMETs address significant convective hazards such as severe thunderstorms.
concepts.apply: Never treat an advisory boundary as a sharp line between perfectly safe and unsafe air.

check.question: Which AIRMET category concerns icing?
check.explanation: AIRMET Zulu describes icing and freezing-level information.

concepts.title: Winds aloft support route planning
concepts.explain: Forecast winds at various altitudes influence groundspeed, endurance, drift, and the choice of cruising altitude.
concepts.apply: A stronger headwind can change fuel reserve and arrival time.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-9 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Temperature aloft matters
concepts.explain: Forecast temperature helps evaluate altitude, aircraft performance, icing possibility, and atmosphere conditions.
concepts.apply: Cold temperatures at cruising altitude may call for icing analysis when moisture is present.

concepts.title: Time window and forecast altitude
concepts.explain: Read the forecast’s valid period and altitude columns; the printed numbers do not apply identically at every height or time.
concepts.apply: Do not use tomorrow afternoon’s wind forecast to plan a dawn flight without checking applicability.

concepts.title: Coded wind direction and speed
concepts.explain: The handbook shows coded wind/temperature groups; interpret the code using the product key and any special high-wind conventions.
concepts.apply: Avoid guessing a wind group or decoding the numbers as the wrong units.

concepts.title: Bring winds into the flight plan
concepts.explain: Wind forecasts feed groundspeed, estimated time en route, planned fuel, and alternates. Recalculate as new observations become available.
concepts.apply: A higher-than-planned headwind may prompt a fuel stop before reserves become tight.

check.question: Why examine winds aloft before selecting cruising altitude?
options: They alter groundspeed and fuel planning
check.explanation: Winds aloft affect ground track, time, fuel planning and altitude selection.

title: Reading Surface Analysis and Station Models

concepts.title: The surface analysis is a snapshot
concepts.explain: A surface analysis chart depicts observed pressure systems, fronts, and other broad weather features at a stated valid time.
concepts.apply: It helps explain why conditions at individual reporting stations differ.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-11 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Isobars reveal pressure patterns
concepts.explain: Isobars connect equal pressures. Their spacing provides a clue to the pressure gradient, one factor associated with wind strength.
concepts.apply: Tightly packed lines can indicate stronger wind potential, but local conditions and terrain still matter.

concepts.title: Front symbols
concepts.explain: Fronts mark boundaries between different air masses. Their position and motion influence weather changes along a route.
concepts.apply: Expect changing wind, cloud and precipitation patterns near a front.

concepts.title: Station-model ingredients
concepts.explain: A station model can combine cloud cover, temperature, dew point, wind, pressure, and weather observations in compact symbols.
concepts.apply: Decode the legend before interpreting a chart rather than guessing from symbol colors.

concepts.title: Chart versus forecast
concepts.explain: An analysis chart describes the analyzed atmosphere. A prognostic chart forecasts conditions at a future valid time.
concepts.apply: Use each for its proper time: current system placement versus likely future movement.

check.question: What does a surface analysis chart primarily depict?
options: Observed large-scale weather features at a specified time
A guarantee of tomorrow’s flight weather
check.explanation: A surface analysis is a time-specific summary of pressure, fronts and other observed weather features.

concepts.title: Prognostic means forecast
concepts.explain: Prognostic charts depict predicted weather features at future valid times. This distinguishes them from analyses of current or recent observations.
concepts.apply: For a long flight, inspect charts corresponding to the expected en route times.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-13 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Broad-area weather depiction
concepts.explain: The chapter discusses weather-depiction products highlighting broad IFR, MVFR, and VFR conditions. Product names and availability can change.
concepts.apply: Interpret legends and product dates; do not assume an old chart format is still published unchanged.

concepts.title: Freezing-level guidance
concepts.explain: Forecast charts can help locate freezing levels and possible icing environments. A freezing-level line does not alone describe all icing risk.
concepts.apply: Combine freezing levels with clouds, moisture and aircraft capability.

concepts.title: Surface-front forecasts
concepts.explain: Surface prognostic charts show expected pressure systems and fronts at later forecast horizons.
concepts.apply: A moving front could cross the destination near your arrival time.

concepts.title: Charts need cross-checks
concepts.explain: A broad chart can conceal local variability, airport-level visibility, and fast-changing convective activity.
concepts.apply: Pair the chart with relevant airport forecasts, alerts, and updated reports.

check.question: What is the key difference between analysis and prognostic charts?
options: Analysis shows analyzed conditions; prognostic forecasts future conditions
check.explanation: Use analysis for an observed weather picture and prognostic charts for future expected conditions.

concepts.title: Precipitation is not the whole threat
concepts.explain: Radar can show precipitation intensity, but dangerous thunderstorm turbulence can extend beyond heavy precipitation echoes.
concepts.apply: Do not use a precipitation-only return as the sole criterion for thunderstorm clearance.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-17 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Radar mosaic age
concepts.explain: An onboard or ground-delivered radar mosaic combines data collected and processed at different moments. Display time can conceal additional delay.
concepts.apply: Check product timestamps and expect the actual storm to have moved or intensified.

concepts.title: Storms move and grow
concepts.explain: Convective cells can build, split and move rapidly. A gap observed on a data link display may close before arrival.
concepts.apply: Plan strategic avoidance with generous margins rather than trying to thread cells from stale imagery.

concepts.title: ATC weather assistance
concepts.explain: ATC may provide available weather information and route assistance, but radar weather depiction and controller services have limits.
concepts.apply: Request help early and retain responsibility for the weather decision.

concepts.title: Do not let equipment replace judgment
concepts.explain: A colorful radar display can create unjustified confidence. Combined briefing, interpretation, and conservative decisions matter more.
concepts.apply: If hazards exceed your capabilities, delay, divert, land, or turn around rather than continuing due to a single reassuring display.

check.question: Why is an in-cockpit NEXRAD picture not adequate for threading thunderstorms?
options: It can be delayed and does not show every hazard
check.explanation: Datalink NEXRAD products have latency; storms can change between observation and cockpit display.

concepts.title: What datalink delivers
concepts.explain: Cockpit weather systems may display text observations, forecasts, advisories and radar products. The handbook discusses FIS-B via ADS-B ground broadcast services.
concepts.apply: Understand which products your particular receiver actually supports.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-20 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Product time and transmission delay
concepts.explain: Creation, formatting, transmission, and display may each add latency. The number on the screen may not reflect real atmospheric age.
concepts.apply: Before using an image, verify both the product time and the update characteristics.

concepts.title: Reception limitations
concepts.explain: Ground station coverage, altitude, equipment, and other conditions affect reception. An absent or outdated product cannot be assumed current.
concepts.apply: Check receiver health and product timestamps; a blank screen does not mean clear weather.

concepts.title: Graphical AIRMET/METAR overlays
concepts.explain: Symbols and colored graphics organize information, but are only as useful as their legend, age, and geographic accuracy.
concepts.apply: Open the details behind a symbol instead of treating color as a complete weather briefing.

concepts.title: Strategic, not tactical
concepts.explain: The handbook emphasizes that datalink weather is useful for broad situational awareness rather than close-in storm penetration or tactical maneuvering.
concepts.apply: Use datalink to plan avoidance well ahead of time, not to select a narrow passage between cells.

check.question: What is the most appropriate use of datalink NEXRAD?
options: Substitute for all other weather reports
check.explanation: NEXRAD latency makes it unsuitable as a tactical storm-avoidance sensor.

concepts.title: Start with a weather question
concepts.explain: Before collecting data, identify what could block the flight: ceilings, winds, icing, convection, turbulence, or runway conditions.
concepts.apply: A short local VFR flight and a long cross-country need different briefing emphasis.

image.caption: FAA Handbook Figure 13-21 — original chart or weather-service illustration

concepts.title: Build a timeline
concepts.explain: Compare observations and forecasts for departure, en route, arrival, and a realistic delay or diversion window.
concepts.apply: Conditions that are fine now may deteriorate before your planned landing.

concepts.title: Compare independently
concepts.explain: If airport METARs, TAFs, radar and advisories point to different outcomes, examine timing and coverage before deciding.
concepts.apply: An improving TAF does not erase a fresh report of conditions below your limits.

concepts.title: Apply personal minimums
concepts.explain: Regulatory weather minima are not necessarily appropriate personal limits. Consider proficiency, fatigue, terrain and equipment.
concepts.apply: A legal flight can still present more risk than you should accept.

concepts.title: Maintain an exit plan
concepts.explain: A robust plan includes fuel reserves, usable alternates, divert points, and willingness to cancel or land.
concepts.apply: As conditions change, decide early while multiple safer choices remain.

check.question: One report looks favorable but several others show weather approaching your route. What should you do?
options: Reassess timing and risk using all relevant sources
Rely only on the single favorable report
check.explanation: Good weather decisions synthesize multiple products and account for timing and uncertainty.
